query: For the equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy and its equiatomic quaternary and ternary subsets that are single-phase FCC after thermomechanical processing, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain why their mechanical properties differ during deformation and failure when constituent count alone is inadequate? Specify a controlled comparison, predictions relative to the quinary baseline, the applicable boundary conditions, supporting evidence, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The mechanical property differences among the equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni (quinary) alloy and its quaternary and ternary subsets arise from compositional variations that alter the local chemical short‐range ordering and degree of lattice distortion. These microstructural differences change the ease of dislocation nucleation, mobility, and deformation twinning, thereby producing distinct yield strengths, work hardening rates, and failure modes that cannot be explained by constituent count alone.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic single-phase FCC microstructures obtained via identical thermomechanical processing for the full Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy and its equiatomic quaternary and ternary subsets.
generation.intervention: Perform controlled mechanical deformation tests (e.g., tensile and compression tests) on the quinary, quaternary, and ternary alloys under identical processing, strain rate, and temperature conditions while characterizing the local chemical order and lattice distortion (e.g., via atom probe tomography or high-resolution TEM).
generation.conditions: Tests conducted at room temperature with identical grain size and processing history to ensure that differences are intrinsic to the compositional variations rather than extrinsic processing factors.
generation.structural_mediator: The magnitude and nature of local chemical short-range order and the resulting lattice distortions that affect dislocation behavior.
generation.mechanism: Minor changes in elemental makeup alter the local atomic environments (i.e., short-range order) and the overall lattice distortion. In the quinary alloy, the optimal combination of these factors provides a balanced impediment to dislocation motion and favorable activation of deformation modes (e.g., twinning). In contrast, the reduced constituent alloys exhibit either lower lattice distortion or different ordering, leading to a change in the barrier for dislocation glide and plasticity mechanisms.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the quinary baseline, the quaternary and especially the ternary alloys will exhibit lower yield strengths and reduced work hardening, with possible shifts in the dominant deformation mechanisms (e.g., less pronounced twinning). These changes will manifest as measurable differences in stress–strain curves and failure behavior.
generation.baseline: The quinary equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy, which shows a specific balance of lattice distortion and short-range order that supports its high strength–ductility combination.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies under conditions where the alloys remain single-phase FCC and are processed to similar microstructural states (e.g., similar grain size and dislocation density) with tests performed at comparable strain rates and ambient temperatures.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative effect of variations in short-range order and lattice distortion on specific mechanical properties is not precisely known and might be influenced by additional factors such as grain boundary characteristics or trace impurity effects.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare specimens of the equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy as well as its equiatomic quaternary and ternary subsets ensuring identical FCC microstructures through controlled thermomechanical processing. Perform in situ deformation experiments (using techniques such as high-resolution TEM or digital image correlation) while simultaneously characterizing local chemical order (via atom probe tomography or similar methods).
measurements: Stress–strain curves (yield strength, work hardening rate, ductility)
Quantitative analysis of local chemical short-range ordering and lattice distortion
Observation of active deformation mechanisms (e.g., dislocation slip, twinning) during loading
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the reduced constituent alloys (quaternary and ternary) do not exhibit systematic and correlatable differences in local chemical order or lattice distortion compared to the quinary alloy—and if these microstructural parameters do not align with the observed differences in mechanical performance (i.e., if changes in deformation mechanisms and strength cannot be linked to variations in short-range ordering)—then the hypothesis is falsified.

[ [6] ] and Cantor et al. [ [7] ] in the beginning of this century. Many definitions were proposed for such materials, but in general they consist of multiple (usually at least five) elements in equiatomic or near-equiatomic composition [ [2] ]. This approach is different from the traditional alloy design using one (or maximum two) principal element and other minor elements. The presence of many elements in equiatomic (or near) composition leads to high mixing entropy and thus to many interesting properties [ [2] , [5] ]. One of such effects is the existence of a random solid solution and simple body centered cubic (bcc) or faced centered cubic (fcc) structure. Recently HEAs with hexagonal closed packed (hcp) structure have been reported as well [ [8] , [9] ]. Abstract The microstructure, temperature-dependent mechanical properties and deformation behaviors of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy (HEA) additively manufactured by selective laser melting (SLM) were investigated. SLM-built HEA had a face-centered cubic (FCC) single-phase random solid solution. In addition, SLM-built HEA was composed of epitaxial growth grains, dislocation network and nano-sized oxides. Room- and high-temperature compression tests confirmed that SLM-built HEA has outstanding mechanical properties in all temperature ranges compared to equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEAs reported up to the present. The excellent mechanical properties of SLM-built HEA were achieved with fine grains, high dislocation density and fine precipitates at low temperatures (25 °C to 600 °C), and by high dislocation density and fine precipitates at high temperatures (700 °C or higher). On the other hand, the deformation microstructure showed that slip and deformation twins are the main deformation mechanisms from 25 °C to 600 °C, and slip and partial recrystallization are the main deformation mechanisms above 700 °C.
